title: Smartphone Ownership, Age of Smartphone Acquisition, and Health Outcomes in Early Adolescence
authors: Barzilay R, Pimentel SD, Tran KT, Visoki E, Pagliaccio D, Auerbach RP
source_note: The PDF on file (docs/pdfs/10.1542_peds.2025-072941.pdf, 10 pages) contains ONLY the Supplemental Material: the table of contents, eMethods 1-5, the eMethods references, Supplemental Figure S1 (correlations among outcomes) and Supplemental Figure S2 (distribution of age at first smartphone). The main article text and tables are not in the PDF. Supplemental Tables S1-S28 are in a separate Excel file that is also not on file. The publisher page returned HTTP 403. Every estimate below is copied from the authors' structured abstract (PubMed PMID 41324306, as stored in 00-search/pubmed_results.csv). Estimates that appear only in the main-text tables or the supplemental Excel file could not be extracted. Before this draft is approved, a human coder needs the main article and the Excel supplement to fill in the missing cells and check which model step the abstract ORs come from.

primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 12 on smartphone ownership (yes vs no), fully adjusted (Model 2)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Abstract (Results); main-text table not on file (the Stage 2 note cites Table 1 of the main paper); Supplemental Tables S3-S5 (Excel, not on file); methods in Supplemental eMethods 2-3 (supplement pp. 3-4).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis (Analysis 1) at the ABCD 2-year follow-up assessment (about age 12). Caregiver-reported smartphone ownership and the three health outcomes are measured at the same visit. Each participant contributes one observation, so there are no repeated measures in this specification. A separate repeated-measures version across the 2-, 3- and 4-year follow-ups (Supplemental Tables S23-S25) is listed under excluded_models.
primary_models.sample: ABCD participants with smartphone-ownership data at the 2-year follow-up, N = 10,588 (eMethods 2; abstract). Of these, 6,739 owned a smartphone and 3,849 did not. The ABCD data release is not stated in the available material. Age, sex and race/ethnicity breakdowns are in the main text and Supplemental Table S1, neither of which is on file. Children with extreme BMI z scores (<-4 or >8) were excluded from BMI/obesity analyses, and sleep-duration outliers beyond mean +/- 4 SD were removed (eMethods 1).
primary_models.iv: Smartphone ownership at the 2-year follow-up, reported by the caregiver. Binary: 1 = owns a smartphone (n = 6,739), 0 = does not (n = 3,849; reference).
primary_models.dv: Three binary outcomes at the 2-year follow-up (eMethods 1). (1) Depression: lifetime (past or current) diagnosis of major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) or unspecified depressive disorder from the KSADS-5. (2) Obesity: BMI at or above the CDC sex- and age-specific 95th percentile, from measured height and weight. (3) Insufficient sleep: fewer than 9 hours of night sleep (American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation). Sleep duration came from the youth-reported Munich Chronotype Questionnaire as average nightly sleep across school days and free days. Outcome prevalences are not available in the material on file.

covariates.name: Ownership of other devices
covariates.detail: Tablets, laptops, iPods and smartwatches; Model 2

covariates.name: Pubertal status
covariates.detail: Self-reported at time of assessment, 1-5 Likert scale from prepubertal to post-pubertal; Model 2

covariates.name: Parental monitoring
covariates.detail: Youth-reported mean of 5 Parental Monitoring Scale items, each 1 (never) to 5 (always or almost always); Model 2

primary_models.equation: logit(P(Outcome[i,j]=1)) = b0 + b1*SmartphoneOwnership[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*household_income + b5*parent_education + b6*Black + b7*Hispanic + b8*other_device_ownership + b9*pubertal_status + b10*parental_monitoring + u[j], where u[j] is the random effect(s). The random-effect structure (e.g., site and/or family) is not described in the material on file. b1 is the log-odds ratio for owners vs non-owners.
primary_models.estimation: Mixed-effects logistic regression in R 4.5.0 (eMethods 3). Covariates were added stepwise: Model 1 had age and sex, and Model 2 added the full set. The random effects, weighting, alpha and multiple-comparison correction are not described in the supplement on file. Analytic code is posted at github.com/barzilab1/ABCD_smartphone_health. Sensitivity analyses: (a) fully adjusted models excluding youth with problematic smartphone use, defined as a mean MPIQ score above 5 on the 1-7 scale (Supplemental Table S12; eMethods 4); (b) E-values for the Model 2 logistic models (Supplemental Table S13; eMethods 5); (c) continuous outcomes (BMI, sleep hours, psychopathology; Supplemental Tables S14-S16); (d) repeated measures across 3 timepoints (Supplemental Tables S23-S25). The abstract reports that results were consistent across several sensitivity analyses. No effect-modification tests appear in the material on file.

primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 12 on age of first smartphone acquisition (per year earlier) among owners, fully adjusted (Model 2)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Abstract (Results); main-text table not on file; Supplemental Tables S6-S8 (Excel, not on file); methods in Supplemental eMethods 2-3 (supplement pp. 3-4); age distribution in Supplemental Figure S2 (supplement p. 10).
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis (Analysis 2) at the 2-year follow-up (about age 12), limited to youth who owned a smartphone by that visit. The IV is the caregiver-reported age at first smartphone acquisition, which is retrospective. Outcomes are measured at the 2-year follow-up. Each participant contributes one observation.
primary_models.sample: Smartphone owners at the 2-year follow-up, n = 6,739 (eMethods 2; abstract). Demographic breakdowns are not available in the material on file. Supplemental Figure S2 pools the age-of-onset reports across the 2-, 3- and 4-year waves: median age 11, range 4-15, interquartile range 10-12.
primary_models.iv: Age of first smartphone acquisition in years, reported by the caregiver. Continuous. The abstract expresses the OR per earlier year of acquisition, so the OR is either for 1 year younger or the coefficient was sign-reversed. No SD is reported in the material on file; Figure S2 gives only median 11, IQR 10-12 and range 4-15, pooled across waves.
primary_models.dv: Same three binary outcomes as M1: KSADS-5 depression diagnosis, obesity (BMI at or above the CDC 95th percentile) and insufficient sleep (<9 h, Munich Chronotype Questionnaire), all at the 2-year follow-up.

covariates.name: (same 9 as M1 Model 2)
covariates.detail: Age, sex assigned at birth, household income, parent education, Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, ownership of other devices, pubertal status, parental monitoring

primary_models.equation: logit(P(Outcome[i,j]=1)) = b0 + b1*(earlier age of first smartphone, years)[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*household_income + b5*parent_education + b6*Black + b7*Hispanic + b8*other_device_ownership + b9*pubertal_status + b10*parental_monitoring + u[j]. exp(b1) is reported as the OR for each earlier year of acquisition.
primary_models.estimation: Same as M1: mixed-effects logistic regression in R 4.5.0, stepwise Model 1 then Model 2. The random-effect structure, alpha and multiple-comparison correction are not described in the material on file. Sensitivity analyses are the same as M1: problematic-use exclusion (S12), E-values (S13), continuous outcomes (S17-S19) and repeated measures (S26-S28).

primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 13 on smartphone acquisition in the past year among non-owners at age 12, adjusted for the prior-year outcome (Model 2)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Abstract (Results); main-text table not on file; Supplemental Tables S9-S11 (Excel, not on file); methods in Supplemental eMethods 1-3 (supplement pp. 3-4).
primary_models.design: Prospective analysis over one year (Analysis 3). The sample is limited to youth who did not own a smartphone at the 2-year follow-up (about age 12). The exposure is acquiring a smartphone by the 3-year follow-up. Outcomes are measured at the 3-year follow-up (about age 13), and each model adjusts for the same health measure at the 2-year follow-up. The exposure and outcome are both assessed at the 3-year visit, so the exposure is not strictly before the outcome. Each participant contributes one observation.
primary_models.sample: Youth without a smartphone at the 2-year follow-up, n = 3,486 (eMethods 2; abstract). Of these, 1,546 had acquired a smartphone in the past year and 1,940 had not. Demographic breakdowns are not available in the material on file.
primary_models.iv: Smartphone acquisition between the 2-year and 3-year follow-ups, reported by the caregiver. Binary: 1 = acquired (n = 1,546), 0 = did not (n = 1,940; reference).
primary_models.dv: Binary outcomes at the 3-year follow-up. (1) Clinical-level psychopathology: the KSADS mood module was not given at this wave, so depression was replaced by a youth self-reported Brief Problem Monitor T-score of 65 or higher, covering internalizing, externalizing and attention symptoms (eMethods 1). (2) Insufficient sleep: <9 h on the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire. (3) Obesity: BMI at or above the 95th percentile. According to eMethods 2, all three outcomes were analyzed, but the abstract reports estimates only for psychopathology and insufficient sleep.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: smartphone owner vs non-owner at age 12. M2: per 1 year earlier age of first smartphone acquisition. M3: acquired a smartphone in the past year vs did not, among non-owners at age 12.
d_transformation.notes: All available estimates are adjusted ORs from mixed-effects logistic models and convert to d with Chinn's formula. p0 is not needed for the OR conversion. Outcome base rates are not in the material on file. Transformability is partial for two reasons. (1) Two cells have no number in the material on file: M2 depression and M3 obesity. (2) The M2 d is per 1 year of acquisition age, and no SD of acquisition age is reported (Figure S2 gives only median 11, IQR 10-12, range 4-15, pooled across waves), so it cannot be rescaled to a per-SD contrast. The M1 and M3 d values are binary-group contrasts, which are comparable in kind to paper 156's group contrasts but not to per-SD d values. All numeric estimates come from the abstract, not the main tables. The full text and the Excel supplement are needed to confirm the values and to add p-values and the missing cells.

extraction_flags:
The PDF on file (docs/pdfs/10.1542_peds.2025-072941.pdf) is not the paper. It is only the 10-page Supplemental Material: eMethods 1-5, references, Fig S1 and Fig S2. The main article text and tables are missing. Supplemental Tables S1-S28 are in a separate Excel file that is also missing. The publisher page returned HTTP 403. All 7 numeric ORs and CIs were therefore copied from the authors' structured abstract (PubMed 41324306, in 00-search/pubmed_results.csv). I checked all 7 against that abstract text programmatically and they match exactly.

A human needs the full article and the Excel supplement to check five things:
(1) That the abstract ORs are from Model 2 (fully adjusted) rather than Model 1. I assumed Model 2.
(2) The two cells with no number, M2 age of acquisition to depression and M3 acquisition to obesity. Both are set to sig=false only because the abstract does not name them as associations.
(3) All p-values, outcome prevalences (p0), sample demographics, ABCD release and random-effect structure. None of these appear in the material on file.
(4) Whether the continuous-outcome models (S14-S22), the repeated-measures models (S23-S28) and the problematic-use exclusion sensitivity models (S12) are interpreted in the main text. If so, they should become additional cards.
(5) The M2 insufficient-sleep CI, 1.08 (1.02-1.12), is asymmetric on the log scale. Confirm it against the table.

M3 uses a BPM T-score of 65 or higher (general psychopathology) instead of KSADS depression. In M3 the exposure and the outcome are both assessed at the 3-year visit. No SD is available for age at acquisition, so the M2 d stays per year rather than per SD.
